neurological_exam.additional: DIAGNOSTIC PUZZLE: (1) NEAR-NORMAL MoCA (26/30) — standard cognitive testing may be insensitive for high-functioning individuals with early bvFTD; (2) Prior bipolar disorder diagnosis — behavioral changes easily attributed to psychiatric disease; (3) Father's possible late-onset 'schizophrenia' could be FTD; (4) MRI will be NORMAL (10-15% of bvFTD, especially C9orf72 carriers); (5) FDG-PET may show only SUBTLE frontal changes. The key features that suggest FTD over bipolar decompensation: progressive and unremitting course (not episodic), severe social cognition loss (not typical bipolar), perseverative writing behaviors, and age of onset pattern.

patient.chief_complaint: Behavioral changes, decreased novel productivity, social withdrawal — 18 months; referred by psychiatrist for 'atypical bipolar features'
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. F is a 54-year-old published novelist with a 15-year history of bipolar disorder type II (well-controlled on valproate) and hypothyroidism who is referred by his psychiatrist for neurological evaluation. His psychiatrist refers him with a note: 'progressive behavioral changes that feel different from prior bipolar episodes — patient does not recognize or endorse symptoms; consider organic process.' Over the past 18 months, Mr. F has undergone a behavioral transformation that his former partner (they divorced 2 years ago) and publisher have independently noticed. His publisher, with whom he has had a relationship for 12 years, reports that his correspondence has become strange — he sends the same paragraph from his current manuscript in every email, verbatim, regardless of the question asked. His manuscript, which he has been working on for 3 years, consists of the same 2,000 words rearranged repeatedly. He is unaware that this is unusual and insists the work is 'progressing.' He has posted a series of publicly embarrassing social media messages commenting on strangers' physical appearances and has made several sexually inappropriate advances toward his publisher's assistant, dismissing any attempt to discuss this as 'censorship.' He has developed an extraordinary fixation on a single television crime drama — watching it for 8-14 hours per day and quoting it verbatim in conversations. He is meticulous about eating the same three foods in the same sequence every day. He has lost all interest in the literary community, which was central to his identity and social world. He does not recognize any of these behaviors as problematic. His bipolar disorder has never manifested this way — his prior hypomanic episodes were characterized by rapid speech, reduced need for sleep, and increased creativity, not perseverative repetition and social disinhibition. He has no history of psychosis. His father was institutionalized in his 50s with a diagnosis of 'late-onset schizophrenia' — the presentation timing raises concern for possible FTD misdiagnosed as a psychotic disorder in the pre-neuroimaging era. The NEAR-NORMAL MoCA (26/30) is the most deceptive feature — he presents as largely cognitively intact on brief standardized testing, making organic disease easy to dismiss. This is the canonical early bvFTD case in a high-premorbid-functioning individual with a prior psychiatric diagnosis.

Posterior cingulate and parietal cortex uptake are preserved — a pattern consistent with frontotemporal hypometabolism. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.test_type: Comprehensive neuropsychological evaluation with social cognition focus

findings.finding: STANDARD TESTS (scores near normal, masking real impairment): DKEFS Trails condition 4: 16th percentile (low average but not severely impaired). Standard executive battery: 20th-30th percentile range. MoCA: 26/30 (patient asked to repeat — same score; he can focus when explicitly tested).

SOCIAL COGNITION BATTERY (severely impaired — the key diagnostic finding): Reading the Mind in the Eyes test: 14/36 (<2nd percentile — severely impaired). Faux Pas recognition: 2/10 (<2nd percentile — cannot identify social violations). Theory of Mind tasks: severely impaired (cannot attribute mental states to others). Moral decision-making tasks: utilitarian responses indicating reduced emotional resonance.

ECOLOGICAL VALIDITY TESTS (real-world judgment): Multiple Errands Task: markedly impaired — makes same errors repeatedly, does not self-correct, is unaware of errors. This captures the ecological deficit not visible on structured tests.
Language: Verbal fluency FAS: 21 words (20th percentile — low average). Naming: 54/60 BNT (40th percentile — age-appropriate). No aphasia.

output.impression: Marked dissociation between near-normal standard cognitive testing and severely impaired social cognition and ecological validity. Social cognition testing (Reading the Mind in the Eyes, Faux Pas recognition, Theory of Mind) is severely impaired (<2nd percentile), in the context of largely preserved performance on structured standard tests. Executive function is in the low-average range. Ecological validity testing demonstrates prominent real-world deficit not captured by structured instruments. Findings are consistent with probable behavioral-variant FTD. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: bvFTD misdiagnosed as bipolar disorder: clinical features and diagnostic delay

output.summary: Behavioral variant FTD is frequently misdiagnosed as bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, or personality disorder, with a mean diagnostic delay of 3-5 years. Key clinical features that should trigger neurological re-evaluation in known psychiatric patients: (1) new perseverative/stereotyped behaviors not consistent with prior psychiatric episodes; (2) severe social cognition impairment (Faux Pas, Theory of Mind) — not a feature of bipolar disorder; (3) anosognosia — patient does not recognize or endorse symptoms; (4) progressive and unremitting course rather than episodic bipolar pattern; (5) onset in 50s in previously bipolar patient. Family history of possible 'late-onset schizophrenia' in a first-degree relative may represent undiagnosed FTD. Normal MRI in a patient with behavioral syndrome should trigger FDG-PET and social cognition testing, not reassurance.
